title: Latch-based clock distribution architecture for POWER4
decision: Adopted a latch-based (pulsed-latch) clock distribution network rather than a conventional flip-flop-based clock tree
rationale: Latch-based clocking allowed more flexible timing through the pipeline, simplified clock tree synthesis, and reduced clock skew while accommodating the distributed nature of the large POWER4 die
outcome: Achieved clock skew within target; enabled timing closure at 130nm on a large die
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly frames this as a latch-vs-flipflop choice or just describes the latch-based implementation without framing alternatives; the paper may describe the implementation without stating that flip-flop approaches were considered and rejected

title: ASIC-style design methodology adoption for physical design
where_in_paper: Design methodology / physical design methodology section
decision: Moved toward an ASIC-like physical design flow (synthesis, place-and-route) for significant portions of POWER4 logic, supplemented by custom circuits for critical paths
alternatives_or_rejected: Full custom design for all logic (prior IBM processor approach)
rationale: Processor complexity and transistor count had grown beyond what full custom could manage efficiently; ASIC methodology provided better productivity and predictability for non-critical logic while retaining custom for critical paths (L1 cache, clocking, critical datapath)
outcome: Successful timing closure; productivity gains over prior full-custom approach; good correlation between synthesis estimates and final silicon
weakest_point: The exact stated boundary between what was ASIC-flow vs. custom; I believe the paper states this but may be reconstructing the boundary imprecisely

title: Conservative wire load models for synthesis timing correlation
where_in_paper: Timing methodology / physical design integration section
decision: Used more conservative wire load models in synthesis than historical practice, to account for wire delay becoming significant at 130nm
rationale: Wire delays dominated gate delays at 130nm for long nets; previous generation wire load models were insufficiently accurate, causing correlation problems between pre-layout synthesis and post-layout timing
outcome: Improved correlation between synthesis timing estimates and final timing; better first-pass timing closure
weakest_point: Whether wire load model conservatism was explicitly framed as a discrete design decision or was discussed more subtly; this may be my inference from reading about timing methodology rather than a stated decision point in the paper

title: Structured power grid for power distribution at large die scale
decision: Implemented a structured (regular, grid-based) power distribution network rather than ad-hoc power routing
rationale: Die size and current density required predictable IR drop; structured grid provided uniform power delivery, simplified analysis, and reduced EM risk compared to ad-hoc approaches
outcome: Achieved target IR drop across the die; reliable power delivery at 130nm with acceptable margins
weakest_point: Whether this was a specific decision discussed in this paper or whether it's general IBM design methodology; the companion microarchitecture paper and other POWER4 documentation may contain this; the paper_vs_general flag reflects genuine uncertainty
